p: Apokalypsis means pulling the cover off. One unveiling, singular, and it is of Jesus.
b: The oldest manuscripts call the book "the Apocalypse of John." Apokalypsis means an unveiling, like pulling a cover off something. It is one unveiling, singular. The book's own first words call it "the revelation of Jesus Christ" (1:1). It is first about who Jesus is, and only then about events.

p: "Soon" or "quickly"? Every view has to explain this word.
b: En tachei and tachy can mean "soon" or "quickly." Preterists read "soon for the first readers." Many futurists read "swiftly, once it starts," or "soon on God's clock" (2 Peter 3:8). "The time is near" (1:3; 22:10) is harder to stretch, and every view has to explain it.
orig: ἐν τάχει (en tachei); ταχύ (tachy); ὁ καιρὸς ἐγγύς (ho kairos engys)

p: "Signified": the book tells you on line one that it speaks in pictures.
b: The KJV's "signified" is exact. God "sign-ified" the message, meaning he showed it by signs. Some modern versions say "made it known" (ESV, NIV). That is correct, but it loses the hint. On line one, the book tells you it speaks in pictures.

t: A book meant to be heard
p: One person read it aloud to the whole church. Most listeners could not read.
b: Ancient letters were read aloud in the assembly (Colossians 4:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:27). The blessing is for "the one who reads" (singular) and "those who hear" (plural). Revelation's repeated patterns of sevens, threes and echoes help a listening audience follow it. It is the first of seven "blessed" sayings in the book.

a: who is, who was, and who is coming
p: A Greek expansion of "I AM WHO I AM" from Exodus 3:14.
b: John breaks Greek grammar here: after "from" he writes the name in the nominative case, as if the name cannot be changed. The phrase unfolds Exodus 3:14 ("I AM"), which Jewish interpreters already read as "the one who was, is, and will be." Notice that John says "is coming," not "will be." God's future is an arrival.

p: Probably the Holy Spirit in full, with seven as completeness.
b: The greeting comes from the Father, the seven Spirits, and Jesus Christ, which looks like an early picture of the Trinity. The seven Spirits are later called seven torches (4:5) and the Lamb's seven eyes (5:6), from Zechariah 4:2, 10. Some read them as seven chief angels instead (compare 8:2). Isaiah 11:2 lists the Spirit's gifts (seven in the Greek Old Testament).

a: the ruler of the kings of the earth
p: Three titles of Jesus from one psalm about David’s king.
b: "Faithful witness," "firstborn," and "highest of the kings of the earth" all come from Psalm 89:27, 37. In a world where Caesar claimed to rule the kings of the earth, the opening greeting names a different ruler.

t: Israel’s calling, now given to the church
p: "A kingdom of priests" was God’s word to Israel at Mount Sinai.
b: Exodus 19:6 calls Israel "a kingdom of priests and a holy nation." Revelation applies the phrase to everyone Jesus freed by his blood, "from every tribe and language" (5:9–10). Some see the church taking up Israel's role; others see Gentiles joining Israel's calling, not replacing it (Romans 11:17). Peter does the same with this verse (1 Peter 2:9).

a: He is coming with the clouds
p: A worldwide return, or Christ’s judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70?
b: The verse joins Daniel 7:13 (the son of man coming on clouds) with Zechariah 12:10 (they will look on the one they pierced). Futurists read the visible return of Christ to the whole world. Preterists note that in the Old Testament God "rides on a cloud" to judge a nation (Isaiah 19:1) and read the judgment of Jerusalem. Jesus used the same verses at his trial (Matthew 26:64).

a: All the tribes of the earth
t: "All kindreds of the earth," or of the land?
p: Gē means both "earth" and "land." Which one changes the whole verse.
b: Gē means both "earth" and "land." The verse quotes Zechariah 12:10–12, where the mourners are the families of Israel. Preterists read "all the tribes of the land" and see first-century Judea. Futurists read "all the peoples of the earth" and see a worldwide return. Both are possible Greek.
orig: πᾶσαι αἱ φυλαὶ τῆς γῆς (pasai hai phylai tēs gēs)

p: "Almighty": the Greek Old Testament’s word for "LORD of armies."
b: Pantokratōr means "ruler of all." The Septuagint uses it for the Hebrew "LORD of hosts" (armies). Outside 2 Corinthians 6:18, it appears in the New Testament only in Revelation (nine times). Roman emperors were sometimes praised as rulers of the world. Revelation reserves the word for God.

p: A rocky island off Asia Minor, used by Rome for exile.
b: Patmos is about 13 square miles. Banishment to an island was a known Roman punishment. Early writers (Irenaeus, Eusebius) say John was sent there under Domitian. "The suffering... and the patient endurance" he shares with the readers are what the whole book asks of them.

t: "The Lord’s day" is not "the Day of the Lord"
p: Sunday, the day of the resurrection, not "the Day of the Lord."
b: Kyriakē is an adjective: "the Lord's." Early Christian writers used it for Sunday, the day of the resurrection (Didache 14; Ignatius, To the Magnesians 9). A few readers take it as "the Day of the Lord," the end times. Greek writes that phrase differently: hēmera kyriou (1 Thessalonians 5:2).
orig: ἐν τῇ κυριακῇ ἡμέρᾳ (en tē kyriakē hēmera)

a: someone like a son of man
p: From Daniel 7:13, Jesus’s favorite name for himself.
b: In Daniel 7 "one like a son of man" comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives an everlasting kingdom. John then describes him with features Daniel gives to God himself (white hair, 7:9) and to the angel of Daniel 10:5–6 (gold belt, fiery eyes, bronze legs). The robe and sash are the clothes of a priest (Exodus 28:4).

t: The Ancient of Days walks among the lamps
p: Jesus is given God’s own portrait, then put to work as the temple priest.
b: Daniel 7:9 gives white wool hair to the Ancient of Days, God. John's figure also wears a priest's robe and walks among lampstands, the priest's daily job of trimming the temple lamps (Exodus 27:20–21; Leviticus 24:1–4). My reading: the vision says both "he is God" and "he tends the churches like a priest tends lamps," trimming, refilling, and, if needed, removing one (2:5). The priestly-lamp reading is held by several scholars (e.g. Beale); the link to the threat in 2:5 is my emphasis.

a: A sharp two-edged sword came out of his mouth
p: His weapon is his word.
b: Isaiah 49:2: "He made my mouth like a sharp sword." Isaiah 11:4: "with the breath of his lips he will slay the wicked." Hebrews 4:12: God's word is "sharper than any two-edged sword." Revelation's last battle is won by this sword alone (19:15, 21).

p: In Isaiah, "the first and the last" means "there is no other God."
b: Isaiah 44:6: "I am the first and I am the last; apart from me there is no God." The Lord God calls himself "the Alpha and the Omega" in 1:8, and Jesus says "I am the First and the Last" here and in 22:13. Revelation gives Jesus the titles of God alone.

a: the keys of death and of Hades
p: Greek religion gave these keys to Hecate or Aeacus. Jesus holds them.
b: In Greek and Roman belief the keeper of the underworld's keys was a god such as Hecate or Aeacus, and Hades was the god of the dead. Jesus, who was dead, now holds the keys. It is a bold claim in a city like Ephesus, where Hecate was worshiped. Compare Jesus's words in Matthew 16:18–19.

a: what is happening now, and what will happen after this
p: Many futurists see three parts here: past, present, future.
b: Futurists often read: "what you have seen" = chapter 1; "what is now" = chapters 2–3; "what will happen after this" = 4–22, still future. Others read it as two parts ("what you have seen, both what is and what is to come"), or as a phrase meaning "everything," since the visions mix past, present and future throughout.

p: Angelos means "messenger": an angel, or a human leader?
b: Angelos simply means "messenger." The "angels of the seven churches" may be guardian angels, or human leaders who read the letters aloud. Each letter scolds its "angel" for the church's sins, which some think fits a human pastor better.

p: The greatest city of Asia, home of the temple of Artemis.
b: A port of perhaps 200,000 people. Paul worked there over two years (Acts 19) and warned its elders about false teachers (Acts 20:29–30). The letter praises them for testing false apostles. Tradition says John lived there late in life.

a: you have left the love you had at first
p: Love for Jesus, love for each other, or both?
b: The Greek just says "your first love." Readers debate whether it means love for Christ, love for fellow believers (which can grow cold in a church busy fighting error), or the early zeal of their conversion. The cure is to "do the things you did at first," which suggests actions, not only feelings.

p: Ephesus’s harbor silted up. The city’s site has moved over the centuries.
b: The river Cayster kept filling Ephesus's harbor with silt, and the city had to move more than once. Today the ruins stand miles from the sea. Ancient readers would also have known the temple lamps that a priest could take away. The threat is not loss of salvation for individuals but the end of a church's witness.

p: Probably Christians who said joining in idol feasts was fine.
b: Irenaeus (about AD 180) linked them to Nicolaus, one of the seven deacons (Acts 6:5), though that may be guesswork. The letters connect them with "the teaching of Balaam" (2:14–15). Nikolaos means "conquers the people," and Balaam was explained in Hebrew as "swallows the people," so the two names may be a pair.

p: The first promise of the book points to the last chapter.
b: Genesis 3:22–24 closes the way to the tree of life. Revelation 22:2 shows it again, beside the river. The promises to the seven churches are all fulfilled in chapters 19–22. At Ephesus, where Artemis's temple stood in a sacred grove, the "paradise of God" is a pointed contrast.

t: "Those who say they are Jews and are not"
p: A painful phrase. It was a local conflict, not a verdict on the Jewish people.
b: Smyrna's Christians, many of them Jewish, were being denounced by members of the local synagogue, possibly to the Roman authorities (Jews were exempt from emperor worship, and Christians lost that cover when expelled). John, himself a Jew, says those slanderers are not living up to the name. Sadly, the phrase was later used to justify hatred of Jews, which the text does not support. Paul uses a similar idea in Romans 2:28–29.

p: A short, limited trial, as in Daniel 1.
b: Daniel and his friends were tested for ten days (Daniel 1:12–15). Ten days is a short, measured time with an end. Historicists have read it as ten years of Diocletian's persecution (303–313), or ten Roman persecutions.

p: Smyrna’s ring of hilltop buildings was called its "crown."
b: Ancient writers described the buildings around Mount Pagos as Smyrna's crown. The word here is stephanos, a victor's wreath, not a king's diadem. Smyrna's bishop Polycarp was later burned there (about AD 155).

p: KJV "seat" is thronos, the word used for God’s throne.
b: KJV says "seat." The word is thronos, the same word Revelation uses over 40 times for God's throne. Pergamum had a giant altar of Zeus and was the first city in Asia with a temple to Rome and Augustus (29 BC). The picture is political: two thrones, and you must pick one.
orig: ὁ θρόνος τοῦ Σατανᾶ (ho thronos tou Satana)

p: The prophet who could not curse Israel, so he taught them to sin.
b: In Numbers 22–24 Balaam is hired to curse Israel but can only bless them. Numbers 31:16 says his advice later led Israel to sin with Moabite women and idols at Peor (Numbers 25). Balaam became a byword for selling out God's people for gain (2 Peter 2:15; Jude 11).

p: A jar of manna was kept in the ark, which went missing.
b: Exodus 16:33–34: a jar of manna was kept before the LORD. Jewish tradition said Jeremiah hid the ark (2 Maccabees 2:4–8) and that the Messiah would bring the manna back (2 Baruch 29:8). Those who refuse idol feasts will get heaven's food instead. Compare John 6:31–35.

p: Jurors voted "not guilty" with white stones. Stones were also feast tickets.
b: Several customs fit: a white pebble for acquittal in court; inscribed tokens that admitted guests to banquets; amulets carrying a secret name. All suit Pergamum, a city of courts and feasts. Some also connect the high priest's stones engraved with names (Exodus 28:9–12).

p: A nickname from the queen who led Israel into Baal worship.
b: Queen Jezebel promoted the worship of Baal (1 Kings 16:31; 21:25) and opposed Elijah. The woman at Thyatira probably was a real prophet in the church whom John calls by this name, the way we might call someone "a Judas." Her teaching seems to have allowed members to join guild feasts honoring the gods.

t: "The deep things": a slogan turned around
p: They likely said "the deep things of God." Jesus corrects the label.
b: Paul writes that the Spirit searches "the deep things of God" (1 Corinthians 2:10). Many scholars suggest the Thyatira group claimed secret, deeper knowledge, perhaps arguing that a mature Christian could enter an idol's temple unharmed. My reading: Jesus quotes their slogan and swaps one word, the way the letters elsewhere turn local boasts around ("you say you are rich," 3:17).

p: The promise of Psalm 2, given to the faithful.
b: Psalm 2:8–9: "I will hand you the nations to inherit... You will crush them with an iron rod; you will shatter them like a jar from the potter." In Revelation the same words describe Jesus (12:5; 19:15) and his people. The Greek poimanei literally means "shepherd," so some translate "shepherd them with an iron rod."

p: Venus, the bright herald of dawn. Jesus says he is the star (22:16).
b: Roman generals claimed Venus as their patron, and Roman coins linked the emperor with stars. Numbers 24:17 promises, "A star will march out of Jacob." In 22:16 Jesus calls himself "the bright Morning Star." The promise is not a prize but Jesus himself.

a: You have a reputation for being alive, but you are dead
p: A city living on its past glory, twice captured because no one was watching.
b: Sardis's citadel was thought impossible to capture. Yet it fell to Cyrus in 547 BC and to Antiochus III in 214 BC when soldiers climbed the cliffs at night and found the walls unguarded. "Wake up!" and "I will come like a thief" hit home.

a: I will come like a thief
p: Jesus’s own picture for a coming no one expects.
b: Jesus: "if the master of the house had known during which watch of the night the thief would come, he would have stayed awake" (Matthew 24:43). Paul: "the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night" (1 Thessalonians 5:2). Revelation repeats it at Armageddon (16:15). Here it may mean a coming in judgment on one church, not only the final return.

p: Cities kept rolls of citizens. Names could be struck off.
b: Greek cities kept registers of citizens, and a convicted person's name could be erased. Moses asks God to "wipe me out, please, from your book that you have written" (Exodus 32:32–33). Jesus promises the opposite: "I will never erase." The Greek uses a strong double negative.

p: From Isaiah 22, where a steward receives the palace keys.
b: Isaiah 22:22: "I will place on his shoulder the key to the house of David; what he opens no one can shut, and what he shuts no one can open." Eliakim became the king's chief steward. Jesus holds that authority over who enters the kingdom, just as the "synagogue of Satan" was trying to shut the door on the believers.

a: who say they are Jews and are not
t: "They will bow down at your feet"
p: A reversal of Isaiah, where the nations bow to Israel.
b: Isaiah 60:14 says the oppressors' children "will bow down at your feet," and Isaiah 49:23 says the same. Here the promise is turned around: the local synagogue opponents will acknowledge the (largely Gentile) church. Church-and-Israel views read this differently: as a temporary local conflict (most), as the church inheriting Israel's promises (replacement views), or as Gentiles grafted into Israel (Romans 11).

a: keep you from the hour of testing
p: The key verse for a pre-tribulation rapture, and a famous debate.
b: The Greek is tērēsō ek, "I will keep out of." Pre-tribulation readers say this means removal before the tribulation. Others note that John 17:15 uses the same words, "keep them from the evil one," where Jesus explicitly says he is not asking that they be taken out of the world. So it can mean protection within. Preterists read it as a promise to the Philadelphia church about a coming crisis in their own time.

p: Philadelphia had been shaken by earthquakes. Pillars were often left standing.
b: After the great earthquake of AD 17 Philadelphians feared aftershocks and many lived outside the walls. In ruined cities the pillars are often what stands. Leading citizens were honored with inscribed pillars in temples. Jesus promises a permanent place, with a new name written on it.

p: From Isaiah 65:16, "the God of Amen."
b: Isaiah 65:16 literally speaks of "the God of Amen," usually translated "the God of truth." The same passage promises "new heavens and a new earth" (65:17). "The ruler (or beginning) of God's creation" echoes Colossians 1:15–18, also written to the Lycus Valley.

t: Lukewarm does not mean "better cold than lukewarm"
p: Not "better cold than lukewarm." Hot and cold water were both useful.
b: People often hear: "I'd rather you be cold toward God than lukewarm." The local setting points somewhere else. Hot springs at nearby Hierapolis were good for healing. Cold spring water at Colossae was good to drink. Laodicea's water came by aqueduct, warm and full of minerals, and it made people want to spit. Hot and cold are both good. Lukewarm means useless. (M. J. S. Rudwick and E. M. B. Green, Expository Times, 1958; Craig Koester.)
orig: ψυχρός (psychros, cold), ζεστός (zestos, hot), χλιαρός (chliaros, lukewarm)

a: salve to put on your eyes
t: Laodicea’s gold, wool and eye salve
p: Three things Laodicea was proud of: banks, black wool, and a medical school.
b: Laodicea was a banking city that refused Roman aid after the earthquake of AD 60 (Tacitus, Annals 14.27). It was famous for glossy black wool and had a medical school associated with a "Phrygian powder" used for eyes. Jesus offers better gold, white clothes, and real sight.

a: I am standing at the door and knocking
t: A door to the heart, or to the church?
p: Spoken to a church, it is an invitation to a meal.
b: This is often used to invite one person to faith, and that is a fair application. In context Jesus speaks to a whole church that has shut him out. The image echoes Song of Songs 5:2 ("my beloved is knocking"), and "eat with" points to the Lord's Supper and the wedding supper (19:9). Some futurists read it of the last church age.

a: a door standing open in heaven
p: Some see the church raptured here. The words are spoken to John.
b: Pre-tribulation readers note that the word "church" is not used again until 22:16 and see 4:1 as a picture of the church caught up before the tribulation. Others point out that the call is to John alone, who is "in the Spirit" (4:2), and that the same words are spoken to the two witnesses in 11:12.

p: Ezekiel saw it around the throne, and it recalls God’s promise after the flood.
b: Ezekiel 1:28: "Like the appearance of a rainbow in the clouds on a rainy day, so was the radiance around him." Genesis 9:13–16: the bow is a sign of God's promise never again to destroy the earth by flood. Judgment is about to come from this throne, but mercy surrounds it.

p: Twelve tribes plus twelve apostles? Angels? Priestly leaders?
b: Popular readings: the people of God of both covenants (12 tribes + 12 apostles, matching the city's gates and foundations in 21:12–14); the 24 divisions of priests in 1 Chronicles 24; or a council of angels. Their white clothes and crowns are promised to overcomers (3:5; 2:10).

p: KJV "four beasts," but the Greek means "living ones."
b: The KJV calls the creatures by God's throne "four beasts." The Greek zōa means "living ones." The monster of chapter 13 is a different word, thērion. In 1611 "beast" meant any animal, so the KJV was not wrong for its day. Today it puts God's worshipers and God's enemies under one label. NKJV, ESV, NIV and NASB all say "living creatures."

a: The first living creature was like a lion
p: The strongest of the wild animals, tame animals, birds, and all creatures.
b: A Jewish saying put it this way: the mightiest among birds is the eagle, among tame animals the ox, among wild animals the lion, and over them all is the human (Midrash Rabbah on Exodus 15:1). The creatures represent all creation worshiping God. Irenaeus (about AD 180) matched them to the four Gospels, the start of a long Christian art tradition.

p: The six-winged seraphim sang this in Isaiah 6.
b: Isaiah 6:2–3: seraphim with six wings call to each other, "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts." John combines Isaiah's seraphim with Ezekiel's four-faced creatures (Ezekiel 1:5–10; 10:14). This song became the "Sanctus" in Christian worship.

a: You are worthy, our Lord and God
p: Domitian liked to be called "our lord and god." Here the title goes to the Creator.
b: The Roman historian Suetonius says Domitian had letters issued in the name of "our lord and god" (dominus et deus noster, Domitian 13). Crowds in the arena hailed emperors with "Worthy!" (Latin dignus, Greek axios). The elders lay their crowns down, as client kings did before the emperor.

a: a scroll with writing on both sides
p: Roman wills were sealed by seven witnesses and opened only at the right time.
b: Roman law required a will to be sealed by seven witnesses. Legal deeds were often written inside and summarized outside. Ezekiel's scroll had writing "on the front and back" (Ezekiel 2:9–10). Daniel was told to seal his words "until the time of the end" (Daniel 12:4).

a: the Lion from the tribe of Judah
t: John hears "Lion" and sees a Lamb
p: The book’s key move: power redefined as sacrifice.
b: The elder announces a Lion (Genesis 49:9) and the Root of David (Isaiah 11:1, 10), Israel's warrior-messiah. John turns and sees a slaughtered Lamb. Bauckham calls this the key to the book: the Messiah wins by dying. I'd add that John repeats this hear-then-see pattern in 7:4–9 (he hears 144,000 from Israel's tribes and sees a crowd no one could count), so in both places what he hears is Israel's promise, and what he sees is how that promise is fulfilled.

p: Arnion, "little lamb," "slaughtered" like a sacrifice, yet standing.
b: Arnion is a small word, sometimes "little lamb." Esphagmenon means "slaughtered," a sacrifice word, stronger than "slain." The Lamb stands alive yet still bears the marks. It is the book's main name for Jesus: 29 uses, 28 of them for Christ. The one other use is the land beast, which has horns "like a lamb" (13:11).

p: Complete power and complete knowledge.
b: Horns stand for power and kingship (Daniel 7:24; Psalm 18:2). The seven eyes are "the seven Spirits of God sent out into all the earth," from Zechariah 4:10: "the eyes of the LORD that range throughout the earth." The Lamb is weak-looking and all-powerful at once.

a: gold bowls full of incense, which are the prayers
p: Psalm 141:2: "Let my prayer be set up as incense in front of you."
b: Prayer rising like incense comes from Psalm 141:2. These bowls return in 8:3–5, where the prayers are mixed with fire and thrown to the earth, and the trumpets begin. The world's judgment is God's answer to his people's prayers.

a: every tribe, language, people, and nation
p: Seven times the book lists all humanity in four parts.
b: The fourfold formula (in varying order) appears at 5:9; 7:9; 10:11; 11:9; 13:7; 14:6; 17:15: seven times four. It may echo Genesis 10, where the nations are listed "by their clans, languages, lands, and nations" (10:5, 20, 31). The Lamb's people undo Babel.

a: they will rule on the earth
p: Manuscripts differ. One points to a future kingdom, the other to the present.
b: Some major manuscripts have the future, "they will reign" (Sinaiticus); others the present, "they reign" (Alexandrinus). The KJV says "we shall reign," following a late reading with "us." Premillennialists favor the future (pointing to 20:4–6); amillennialists note the present fits 1:6.

p: Daniel 7:10: "Ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him."
b: The Greek myriades myriadōn is the largest number the language could easily say. It is taken directly from Daniel 7:10, where it surrounds the Ancient of Days at the judgment. A picture of a number beyond counting, not a census.

p: Christ, the gospel, a false Christ, or a conquering empire?
b: Christ or the gospel (Irenaeus, many historicists), because Christ rides a white horse in 19:11. A false Christ (many futurists), because Jesus warned that deceivers come first (Matthew 24:4–5). Conquest itself, the first of four disasters. The bow suggests the Parthians, the mounted archers Rome feared.

a: A quart of wheat for a full day
t: "A measure of wheat for a penny"
p: Not cheap: a full day’s pay for one person’s bread.
b: A dēnarion was a full day's pay for a worker (Matthew 20:2). A choinix, about a quart, was one person's daily ration. So the rider announces a whole day's wage for one person's bread: famine prices, many times the normal cost. "Penny" makes it sound cheap. NIV: "two pounds of wheat for a day's wages."

a: don't harm the olive oil and the wine
p: In AD 92 Domitian ordered vineyards cut back, then backed down.
b: Suetonius (Domitian 7, 14) says Domitian, during a grain shortage, ordered half the vineyards in the provinces destroyed, but cancelled the order after protests, possibly from Asia. Whether or not John had this in mind, the picture is of a famine where basic grain is scarce while luxury goods continue.

p: Chlōros: the gray-green color of a corpse.
b: Chlōros (the root of "chlorophyll") means pale green, the gray-green of a corpse. Revelation uses the same word for green grass in 8:7 and 9:4.

a: sword, famine, disease, and the wild animals
p: Ezekiel 14:21: "my four dreadful judgments: sword, famine, wild beasts and plague."
b: The fourth rider's list is borrowed from Ezekiel 14:21, and follows the covenant curses of Leviticus 26:21–26. The horsemen are not random disasters; they are the old covenant warnings coming to pass.

p: Sacrificial blood was poured at the base of the altar.
b: In the temple, the blood of a sacrifice was poured out at the base of the altar (Leviticus 4:7). The martyrs are pictured as sacrifices. Paul calls his coming death being "poured out like a drink offering" (2 Timothy 4:6).

p: The cry of the psalms of lament.
b: "How long?" is the prayer of Psalm 13:1–2; 79:5–10; 94:3 and Zechariah 1:12. Psalm 79:10 asks God to let the nations see "the vengeance for your servants' blood that was spilled." The rest of the book is the answer to this question (see 10:6, "no more delay").

a: the whole moon turned red like blood
p: Joel 2:31: "The sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood."
b: The cosmic signs come from Joel 2:31 and Isaiah 13:10; 34:4 (the sky rolled up like a scroll). In Isaiah these signs announce the fall of Babylon and Edom, real historical judgments, described in world-ending language. Futurists expect literal events; preterists and idealists read prophetic "collapse of the world order" language. Some today connect "blood moons" (lunar eclipses) to these verses.

p: Hosea 10:8, and Jesus’s words on the way to the cross.
b: Hosea 10:8: "They will say to the mountains, 'Cover us!' and to the hills, 'Fall on us!'" Jesus quotes it to the women of Jerusalem in Luke 23:30, warning of the city's coming destruction. Preterists see that link as support for a first-century focus.

p: A deliberately strange phrase. Lambs are not angry.
b: No ancient reader would expect anger from a lamb. My reading: the phrase holds together two things the book will not separate. The judge is the one who was slaughtered for the people now hiding. His anger is the anger of rejected love, not of a tyrant. This fits 14:10, where the torment happens "in front of the Lamb."

p: A figure of speech for the whole world, still used today.
b: Isaiah 11:12 speaks of "the four corners of the earth" too. Ancient writers used it as we use "the four corners of the globe." The four winds are agents of judgment (Jeremiah 49:36; Zechariah 6:5).

p: Ezekiel 9: a mark on those who grieve over sin protected them.
b: In Ezekiel 9:4–6 a man in linen marks the foreheads of the faithful in Jerusalem before the city's judgment. The Hebrew mark is the letter tav, which in old script looked like an X or a cross. The beast's mark in chapter 13 is a counterfeit of this seal.

p: Jewish believers, the whole church, or a special group?
b: Ethnic Israel: Jewish believers in the end times (many futurists). The whole people of God, pictured as Israel's army (many amillennialists), since the crowd John sees next is the same group. Jewish Christians of the first century (some preterists). A literal number of an elite group (Jehovah's Witnesses).

p: Judah first, Dan and Ephraim missing.
b: There are about 20 tribal lists in the Old Testament, and this one matches none. Judah, the tribe of the Messiah, comes first instead of Reuben. Dan is missing; Irenaeus thought the antichrist would come from Dan (Jeremiah 8:16; Genesis 49:17), and Dan was linked to idolatry (Judges 18; 1 Kings 12:29). Ephraim is absent but Joseph is named. Levi, usually left out of military lists, is included.

a: a huge crowd that no one could count
t: The promise to Abraham, counted and uncountable
p: 144,000 is what John hears. What he sees is Abraham’s uncountable family.
b: God told Abraham to "number the stars, if you can number them... So will your offspring be" (Genesis 15:5) and "too many to count" (Genesis 16:10; 32:12). The census in 7:4–8 is a military muster like Numbers 1. My view, following Bauckham: the crowd is the same group as the 144,000, seen as it truly is, Abraham's promise fulfilled through every nation, just as John heard "Lion" and saw "Lamb" in chapter 5.

p: Waved at the Feast of Tabernacles and at victories.
b: Palm branches were used at the Feast of Tabernacles (Leviticus 23:40), at the victory celebrations of the Maccabees (1 Maccabees 13:51; 2 Maccabees 10:7), and at Jesus's entry into Jerusalem (John 12:13). 7:15 says God will "spread his tent over them," another Tabernacles echo.

p: One future seven-year period, or the suffering of the whole church age?
b: The Greek has the article: "the great tribulation," as in Daniel 12:1 and Matthew 24:21. Futurists see a specific future period, and this crowd as people saved during it. Preterists see the war of AD 66–70 and the persecutions of the time. Idealists note John says he already shares "the suffering" (1:9) with his readers.

a: washed their robes and made them white in the blood
p: A paradox: red blood makes white robes.
b: The image draws on Exodus 19:10, 14, where the people wash their clothes before meeting God at Sinai, and on Isaiah 1:18: "though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow." The blessing in 22:14 repeats it.

a: God will wipe every tear from their eyes
p: Isaiah 25:8: "The Sovereign LORD will wipe away the tears from all faces."
b: Isaiah 25:6–8 describes a feast for all peoples on God's mountain, where death is swallowed up forever and tears are wiped away. Revelation uses this promise here and again in 21:4. Verse 16 quotes Isaiah 49:10, and the Lamb as shepherd recalls Psalm 23.

a: silence in heaven for about half an hour
p: Jewish tradition said heaven’s songs paused so that Israel’s prayers could be heard.
b: Habakkuk 2:20 and Zephaniah 1:7 call for silence before the LORD's judgment. In temple worship, the burning of incense came in a hush while the people prayed (Luke 1:10). Some later rabbinic traditions say the angels fall silent so Israel's prayers can be heard (b. Hagigah 12b). Many commentators connect these. My suggestion: the "half hour" is the length of the evening incense offering, during which the people stood outside praying. The next verses show exactly that offering.

a: threw it down to the earth
p: Ezekiel 10: coals from between the cherubim scattered over Jerusalem.
b: In Ezekiel 10:2 a man in linen fills his hands with burning coals from among the cherubim and scatters them over the city. The prayers of 6:10 rise, and the answer comes down as fire.

a: Hail and fire mixed with blood
p: The trumpets copy the plagues of Exodus.
b: Hail and fire (Exodus 9:23–25), water to blood (Exodus 7:20), darkness (Exodus 10:21), locusts (Exodus 10:12–15). The trumpets and bowls retell the Exodus on a world scale, with the beast's kingdom as Egypt and the church as Israel leaving it.

p: Limited judgment: a warning, not yet the end.
b: Trumpet judgments strike "a third" again and again (12 times in chapter 8). The bowls later strike everything. The partial strikes are warnings that leave room to repent, which 9:20–21 says people refused to do. Compare Ezekiel 5:2, 12, where Jerusalem's people are divided into thirds.

a: a huge mountain on fire was thrown into the sea
p: Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, and a writer of the time described it in similar terms.
b: Some scholars note that Vesuvius's eruption, which buried Pompeii, was described as a burning mountain, and the Sibylline Oracles (4.130–136) treat it as God's punishment of Rome. Jeremiah 51:25 calls Babylon a "burned-out mountain." Others read the mountain as a fallen kingdom, since mountains often stand for kingdoms in prophecy.
l: Eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD
Eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD

p: A bitter plant, used by the prophets for judgment.
b: Jeremiah 9:15: "I will make this people eat wormwood and drink poisoned water." Many people linked this verse to Chernobyl (1986), because the Ukrainian word names a related plant (mugwort).

p: KJV says "an angel," but the oldest manuscripts say "an eagle."
b: The Textus Receptus reads "angel," and so does the KJV. Nearly all early manuscripts read "eagle." Eagles (or vultures, the same Greek word) gather over the dead (Matthew 24:28), and Hosea 8:1 pictures an eagle over God's house with a trumpet to the lips.

p: Satan, a fallen angel, or simply an angel sent down?
b: The Greek is a perfect tense, "had fallen," which suggests the star fell before John saw it. Isaiah 14:12 describes the fall of the "morning star." Jesus says, "I was watching Satan fall like lightning out of heaven" (Luke 10:18). Others note that 20:1 has a good angel holding the same key, and read this star as an angel sent on a mission.

p: Joel 2 describes an invading army as locusts that look like horses.
b: Joel 1–2: a locust swarm "like horses" with teeth "of a lion," sounding "like the noise of chariots." Joel used a real locust plague to picture an invading army and the Day of the LORD. Readers have seen in these locusts Muslim armies (historicists), modern attack helicopters (some futurists), Roman armies (preterists), or demonic torment (idealists).

p: The life span of a locust, or the length of the locust season.
b: Locusts typically live about five months, and the dry season when they swarm (May to September) is about that long. Some preterists connect it to the five months of Gessius Florus's violence in AD 66, or to the five months of the Roman siege of Jerusalem in AD 70.

p: Hebrew "Destruction," Greek "Destroyer." A jab at Apollo?
b: Abaddon is a Hebrew word for the place of destruction (Job 26:6; Proverbs 15:11). The Greek name Apollyōn sounds like Apollo, whose symbols included the locust. Emperors such as Nero and Domitian liked to be associated with Apollo. Many scholars think John is mocking the emperor's patron god.

p: The eastern border of Rome, and beyond it the feared Parthians.
b: The Euphrates was the boundary between the Roman Empire and the Parthian Empire. Parthian horse-archers could shoot backward while riding, which may explain power "in their tails" (9:19). Rumors that Nero would return leading a Parthian army spread in the decades after his death.

p: A literal army from Asia, or a number meaning "beyond counting"?
b: The Greek is "two myriads of myriads," twice the "ten thousand times ten thousand" of 5:11. Some futurists have pointed to China, which once claimed a militia of 200 million. Most others read an uncountable demonic host.

a: did not turn away from what their hands had made
p: The prophets’ mockery of idols, and Pharaoh’s hard heart.
b: The list of gold, silver, bronze, stone and wood idols that cannot see, hear, or walk comes from Daniel 5:23 and Psalm 115:4–7. Like Pharaoh after each plague (Exodus 8:15), people refuse to repent. Judgment in Revelation is aimed at repentance, which is why its failure is noted.

p: The root of "pharmacy," but here it means magic and potions.
b: Pharmakeia meant mixing potions, poisons and spells. Some modern preachers read it as drug use or even the medical industry. In ancient usage it is about magic. It returns in 18:23, where Babylon deceives the nations by her pharmakeia.

p: His face like the sun and feet like fire match Jesus in chapter 1.
b: The cloud, rainbow, face like the sun and legs of fire echo 1:15–16 and the throne of 4:3. Some (especially older historicists) take him to be Christ. Most note he is called "another angel," swears by God rather than by himself, and resembles the angel of Daniel 10–12.

a: Seal up what the seven thunders said
p: The one secret in an unsealed book.
b: Some think the thunders were a series of judgments God decided to skip, in mercy (Bauckham). Others take it as a warning to humble interpreters: not everything is revealed (Deuteronomy 29:29). Psalm 29 describes "the voice of the LORD" as thunder seven times.

a: There will be no more delay
p: KJV "time no longer" is not about the end of time.
b: KJV: "that there should be time no longer." This has often been preached as "time itself will end and eternity begins." In context the angel is answering the martyrs' cry, "How long?" (6:10). Chronos here means a waiting period. NKJV, ESV, NIV and NASB: "There will be no more delay." The scene answers Daniel 12:7, where an angel swears how long the waiting will be.

a: the mystery of God will be finished
t: The mystery announced to the prophets
p: Amos 3:7: "God does nothing without revealing his plan to his servants the prophets."
b: The angel's words echo Amos 3:7 and Daniel 12:7. In the New Testament "mystery" means God's plan once hidden and now revealed: Christ, and Gentiles joined with Israel (Ephesians 3:3–6; Romans 16:25–26).

p: Ezekiel ate a scroll that tasted like honey.
b: Ezekiel 3:1–3: "Eat this scroll; then go and speak to the people of Israel... It tasted as sweet as honey in my mouth." Ezekiel's scroll was full of "lament and mourning and woe" (2:10). God's word is sweet to receive and painful to carry.

p: Herod’s temple before AD 70, a future rebuilt temple, or the church?
b: Preterists: the temple still stood when John wrote, so this was written before AD 70 and describes the siege. Futurists: a rebuilt third temple during the tribulation. Idealists and many others: the church as God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16), protected inwardly while its outer life is trampled. Measuring signals protection, as in Ezekiel 40–42 and Zechariah 2:1–5.

p: Revelation names 3½ years in several ways, but never "seven years."
b: Revelation names a 3½-year period in several ways: 42 months, 1,260 days, and "a time, times and half a time." The seven-year tribulation comes from joining these to the "one week" of Daniel 9:27. That can be argued, but the number seven is built from Daniel, not stated in Revelation.
orig: μῆνας τεσσεράκοντα δύο (42 months); ἡμέρας χιλίας διακοσίας ἑξήκοντα (1,260 days)

a: They will trample the holy city
p: Jesus: "Jerusalem will be trampled by Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled."
b: Luke 21:24 uses the same words. Daniel 8:13 also speaks of the sanctuary being trampled. Preterists read the Roman siege; futurists a future occupation; idealists the church's suffering in the world.

a: the two olive trees and the two lampstands
p: In Zechariah 4 the two olive trees are a king and a priest.
b: Zechariah 4:3, 11–14: two olive trees feed oil to a lampstand; they are "the two anointed ones who serve the Lord of all the earth," probably Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest. In Revelation the two witnesses are also two lampstands, which in 1:20 stand for churches.

p: One shuts the sky like Elijah, the other turns water to blood like Moses.
b: Elijah stopped the rain (1 Kings 17:1) and called down fire (2 Kings 1:10). Moses turned water to blood (Exodus 7:20). Malachi 4:5 promised Elijah's return, and Moses and Elijah appear with Jesus at the transfiguration (Mark 9:4).

p: "Where their Lord was crucified" sounds like Jerusalem. But "the great city" is Babylon everywhere else.
b: Preterists read Jerusalem: "where their Lord was also crucified." Others note that "the great city" is always Babylon later (16:19; 17:18; 18:10) and that John says it is called Sodom and Egypt "symbolically" (literally "spiritually"). On that reading it is the world's city, which crucified Jesus through Rome's governor.

p: The book of Esther ends with feasting and sending gifts after enemies are killed.
b: Esther 9:19–22 describes the Jewish festival of Purim, celebrated with "feasting and sending gifts to one another," after the enemies of God's people were defeated. Here the world celebrates the death of God's prophets in exactly those words. My suggestion: the scene is a deliberate inversion of Purim, and like Esther, the celebration is reversed in a moment (11:11).

p: The same words as 4:1. Some see a mid-tribulation rapture here.
b: Mid-tribulation readers see the church (pictured by the witnesses) raised and caught up halfway through, before the seventh trumpet, linking it to Paul's "last trumpet" (1 Corinthians 15:52). Others see a vindication scene modeled on Jesus's own resurrection and ascension.

a: The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom
p: The best manuscripts have one kingdom, the world’s, which changes hands.
b: KJV: "The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord." The oldest manuscripts have the singular: "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ." The world is pictured as one kingdom, the beast's, which changes hands.
orig: ἡ βασιλεία (singular) vs αἱ βασιλεῖαι (plural, Textus Receptus)

p: Missing since 586 BC. Here it is seen in heaven.
b: The ark disappeared when Babylon destroyed Solomon's temple. 2 Maccabees 2:4–8 says Jeremiah hid it in a cave until God gathers his people again. Revelation's answer: the true ark was always in heaven. Various groups have claimed to have it, including the Ethiopian Orthodox Church in Aksum.

a: a woman dressed in the sun
p: Israel, Mary, the church, or all three?
b: Israel: the sun, moon and twelve stars come from Joseph's dream of his family (Genesis 37:9), and Israel "gives birth" to the Messiah (Isaiah 66:7–8; Micah 5:3). Mary: she literally bore the child (a common Catholic and Orthodox reading). The church: her other children are believers (12:17). Many readers see the faithful people of God across both covenants.

p: Goddesses were pictured crowned with stars. So was the European flag.
b: Ancient goddesses such as Isis and the Roman Juno were shown as queens of heaven with stars and the moon. John's woman is the true queen-mother. The circle of twelve gold stars on the European flag (1955) was partly inspired, by its designer's later account, by images of Mary based on this verse.

a: a huge red dragon with seven heads
p: Canaanite texts describe Litan, "the mighty one with seven heads."
b: At Ugarit (about 1300 BC) Baal defeats Litan, "the twisting serpent, the mighty one with seven heads." The Old Testament calls this monster Leviathan and says God crushed its heads (Psalm 74:13–14; Isaiah 27:1). Babylon's Tiamat and Greek Typhon are similar chaos monsters.

t: A third of the angels fell?
p: A popular belief, but the text may mean something else.
b: Many Christians believe a third of the angels followed Satan in a rebellion before creation, based on this verse. The verse is placed at the birth of Christ, and it echoes Daniel 8:10, where a horn (Antiochus) throws down some of the stars, meaning God's people. The idea of a pre-creation fall comes more from later tradition (and Milton's Paradise Lost) than from this text.

t: Revelation never uses "rapture" for the church
p: The book’s only "rapture" (harpazō) is Jesus’s own ascension.
b: "Rapture" comes from the Latin of 1 Thessalonians 4:17 (rapiemur, "we will be caught up"). Revelation uses harpazō only once, for the male child, Jesus, "caught up to God and to his throne" (12:5). Pre-tribulation readers find the church's rapture implied at 4:1, "Come up here." Those words are spoken to John alone. The same words are spoken again in 11:12, to the two witnesses after they rise from the dead.

a: She gave birth to a son
p: In Greek myth a dragon hunted a pregnant goddess. Ephesus told this story.
b: The dragon Python hunted the pregnant Leto to keep her from bearing Apollo. She escaped (helped by the north wind or Poseidon) and gave birth on an island. Apollo later killed Python. Ephesus claimed the birth happened nearby, and Roman emperors presented themselves as Apollo. Many scholars think John retells the myth with Jesus as the real dragon-slayer.

p: In Daniel, the great prince who protects Israel.
b: Daniel 10:13, 21; 12:1: Michael is "the great prince who protects your people," who arises in a time of great distress. Jude 9 calls him the archangel. In Revelation the war is won in heaven, but 12:11 says the real victory came "by the blood of the Lamb."

p: The dragon is the snake of Genesis 3, finally exposed.
b: Revelation names the serpent of Genesis 3 as the devil, a link the Old Testament never makes outright (compare Wisdom 2:24 and Romans 16:20). Genesis 3:15 promised that the woman's offspring would crush the serpent's head; chapter 12 shows a woman, a child, and the serpent.

p: The Hebrew satan is a prosecutor, as in Job and Zechariah.
b: In Job 1–2 and Zechariah 3:1, "the satan" is the accuser in God's court. Diabolos (devil) means "slanderer." John's Greek word katēgōr is a legal term borrowed into Hebrew and Aramaic as well. After Christ's victory, the prosecutor loses his place in court (compare Romans 8:33–34).

a: They defeated him by the blood of the Lamb
p: The war in heaven is won on earth, by a cross and by testimony.
b: Verses 7–9 show an angelic war; verses 10–11 reveal how it was really won: by the Lamb's blood, by believers' testimony, and by their refusal to love their lives. My reading: Michael's battle is the heavenly side of the cross, which explains why it happens right after the child is "snatched up" (12:5). Jesus links his death with Satan being "thrown out" in John 12:31–32.

a: two wings of a great eagle
p: God said he lifted Israel up "on the wings of eagles."
b: Exodus 19:4: "I lifted you up on the wings of eagles and brought you to me." Deuteronomy 32:11 pictures God as an eagle spreading its wings over its young. The woman's flight into the wilderness, where she is fed, retells Israel's Exodus and manna. Some preterists see the Jerusalem church fleeing to Pella before AD 70 (Eusebius 3.5.3).

a: a time, times, and half a time
p: Daniel 7:25 and 12:7: three and a half "times."
b: The phrase comes from Daniel 7:25 and 12:7. Here it equals the 1,260 days of 12:6, which shows that John treats the different phrases as one period.

p: In the Exodus story, the earth swallowed Pharaoh’s army and later Korah.
b: Exodus 15:12 says of Pharaoh's army at the sea: "the earth swallowed them." Numbers 16:32: "the earth opened its mouth and swallowed" Korah's rebels. Creation itself takes the side of God's people.

a: a beast coming up out of the sea
p: Leopard, bear and lion, the beasts of Daniel 7, combined.
b: Daniel 7:3–7 sees four beasts rise from the sea: a lion, a bear, a leopard, and a terrible fourth beast with ten horns. John's beast combines all four, in reverse order. Daniel's beasts are kingdoms (7:17). In John's time, the empire combining all earlier empires was Rome.

p: Not the "living creatures" of chapter 4. A wild, hunting animal.
b: Thērion is a wild or dangerous animal, used for animals in the arena where Christians were killed. The word appears 38 times in Revelation, all for the beasts of chapters 11–20. The heavenly creatures of chapter 4 are zōa, "living ones."

p: Rumors said Nero had not died, or would return from the dead.
b: Nero killed himself in AD 68 with a sword wound to the throat. Rumors spread that he was alive in the East and would return; at least three impostors appeared (Tacitus, Histories 2.8; Suetonius, Nero 57). Others link the healed head to Rome surviving the chaos of AD 69. Futurists expect a future ruler who survives or fakes a fatal wound.

t: A counterfeit of "Who is like God?"
p: The people’s cry parodies Israel’s song, and the name Michael.
b: "Who is like you among the gods, O LORD?" was Israel's song after the Red Sea (Exodus 15:11). The name Michael means "Who is like God?" Many scholars note the parody of Exodus 15. My addition: placed just after Michael's victory in chapter 12, the crowd's question "Who is like the beast?" answers Michael's own name with the wrong answer.

p: "Was given," "was allowed": the beast’s power is on loan, for a set time.
b: The verb "was given" appears again and again in chapter 13 (verses 5, 7, 14, 15). The beast's authority comes from the dragon (13:2), but the time limit comes from God. Forty-two months echoes Israel's 42 camps in the wilderness (Numbers 33).

t: What happened "since the world was made"?
p: Names written since creation, or the Lamb slain since creation?
b: The Greek word order allows "the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world" (KJV, NIV) or "names written from the foundation of the world" (ESV, NRSV). 17:8 uses the same phrase with names written in the book, which favors the second.

a: another beast coming up out of the earth
p: Later called "the false prophet." It looks like a lamb, but speaks like a dragon.
b: Readers have seen: the priests of the imperial cult in Asia (preterists, many scholars); the papacy (Reformers); a future religious leader (futurists); or any religion that serves state power (idealists). From the 1850s, Seventh-day Adventist writers identified it with the United States, a "lamb-like" young nation with two horns (civil and religious liberty).

p: Ancient temples had statues that seemed to speak, and priests who staged wonders.
b: Ancient writers describe hollow statues that "spoke" and tricks that made fire appear. Lucian (2nd century) mocked the false prophet Alexander, who made a snake-god appear to speak. In Asia, cities competed to build imperial temples with large emperor statues.

a: a mark on their right hand or on their forehead
p: The Greek says "on," not "in." Charagma was a stamp or seal.
b: KJV: "to receive a mark in their right hand, or in their foreheads." The Greek epi means "on." The English "in" has fed ideas about implanted chips. Charagma was the word for a stamp: the emperor's image on a coin, or an official seal on a sales contract. The mark copies God's seal on the forehead (7:3; 14:1) and the command to bind God's word on the hand and forehead (Deuteronomy 6:8).
orig: χάραγμα ἐπὶ τῆς χειρὸς (charagma epi tēs cheiros)

a: no one can buy or sell
p: Guild membership and markets were tied to the worship of patron gods and the emperor.
b: In cities like Thyatira, trade guilds held feasts honoring patron gods, and markets displayed the emperor's image. Roman coins bore his image and titles. Refusing to take part could cost a Christian their livelihood, a kind of pressure the letters of chapters 2–3 already describe.

p: Some ancient copies read 616. Either way, it fits "Nero Caesar" in Hebrew letters.
b: Most manuscripts read 666. But Papyrus 115 (third century, the oldest copy of this verse) and Codex Ephraemi (fifth century) read 616. Irenaeus, around AD 180, knew both and defended 666. In Hebrew letters, "Nero Caesar" spelled נרון קסר adds up to 666. Spelled the Latin way, נרו קסר, it adds up to 616. That fit is why many scholars think the first readers heard "Nero."

p: Psalm 2: "I myself have put my king in place on my holy mountain, on Zion."
b: Psalm 2:6 sets God's anointed king on Zion against the rebellious nations, which is exactly the contrast with chapter 13. Joel 2:32: "on Mount Zion there will be deliverance." Hebrews 12:22 speaks of "the heavenly Jerusalem," Mount Zion, as something believers have already come to.

a: his Father's name written on their foreheads
p: Chapter 13 marks people with the beast’s name. Chapter 14 shows God’s.
b: The two chapters are set side by side: the beast's mark and name (13:16–17) versus the Lamb's and Father's names (14:1). The high priest wore "Holy to the LORD" on his forehead (Exodus 28:36–38). Everyone belongs to someone.

a: did not make themselves impure with women
p: A soldier’s purity before holy war? Faithfulness without idolatry?
b: The 144,000 "were not defiled with women, for they are virgins." Parthenos is usually used of women but here describes men. Many scholars read it as the purity rule for soldiers in holy war (Deuteronomy 23:9–10; 1 Samuel 21:5), which fits the army-style census of chapter 7. Others read faithfulness with no idolatry, which the prophets call adultery. A few read literal celibacy.

p: The first part of the harvest, given to God, promising more to come.
b: Firstfruits were the first sheaves offered at the feast before the full harvest (Leviticus 23:10). James 1:18 calls believers "a kind of firstfruits of all he created." In this chapter, a full harvest follows (14:14–16).

p: A last call to repent. Seventh-day Adventists see their mission here.
b: The first angel calls every nation to "fear God and give him glory" and worship the Creator. Adventist tradition reads 14:6–12 as God's last message, centered on the Sabbath (Exodus 20:11). Most others read a final offer of grace to all nations before the harvest.

a: Fallen! Fallen is Babylon the Great
p: "Babylon has fallen, has fallen!" (Isaiah 21:9).
b: The cry is from Isaiah 21:9, and "Babylon the great" from Daniel 4:30, where Nebuchadnezzar boasts of the city he built. Jeremiah 51:7: "Babylon was a gold cup in the LORD's hand; she made the whole earth drunk."

a: The smoke of their torment rises forever and ever
p: Eternal conscious punishment, final destruction, or symbol?
b: Traditional readers see eternal conscious punishment. Others (conditional immortality, or "annihilationism") note that the image is copied from Isaiah 34:10, where Edom's smoke "rises forever" but the land is then inhabited by wild animals, so the image means complete, permanent destruction. A third group stresses that the scene is a warning meant to lead to repentance (14:7, 12).

a: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord
p: The second blessing of the book, for martyrs and all believers.
b: "Rest" answers 14:11, where the beast's worshipers have "no rest." The verse echoes Hebrews 4:9–10 on entering God's rest. It is often read at Christian funerals.

a: someone like a son of man
p: Christ, gathering his people? Or an angel of judgment?
b: The "son of man" on a cloud with a gold crown seems to be Christ (1:13; Daniel 7:13). The grain harvest may picture the gathering of believers (Matthew 13:30; Mark 4:29); the grape harvest that follows is judgment. Some read both harvests as judgment. Notice that an angel tells him when to reap, as Jesus said only the Father knows the hour (Mark 13:32).

p: The Greek gives 1,600 stadia. Like most numbers here, it carries meaning.
b: A stadion was about 607 feet, so 1,600 stadia is about 184 miles. The number is 40 × 40 or 4 × 4 × 100, both suggesting the whole world. Some point out it is close to the length of Israel from Tyre to the border of Egypt. Converting it to miles hides the pattern, so most literal translations keep "stadia."

a: a sea of glass mixed with fire
p: Israel sang beside the sea after Pharaoh’s army drowned.
b: Exodus 15: having crossed the sea, Moses and Israel sing. Here the conquerors of the beast stand beside a sea of glass and sing "the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb." The fire may suggest judgment or the pillar of fire.

a: the song of God's servant Moses and the song of the Lamb
t: A song of Moses that never mentions their own victory
p: Exodus 15 celebrates Israel’s rescue. This song celebrates God and the nations.
b: Exodus 15 sings of Israel's escape and the enemy drowned. Remarkably, the song in Revelation 15:3–4 never mentions the singers' victory at all. It quotes Psalm 86:9 and Jeremiah 10:7 and ends with "all nations will come and worship." Bauckham noticed this. My addition: since the beast's followers just heard a call to repent (14:6–7), the song of the saved is about the nations turning to God, not about their own triumph.

p: The tabernacle in the wilderness, where the covenant tablets were kept.
b: The "tent of the testimony" (Numbers 9:15; 17:7) held the ark and the tablets of the law. Judgment comes from the place of God's covenant. The smoke filling the temple recalls Exodus 40:34–35 and Isaiah 6:4.

p: Sores, blood, darkness: the plagues of Egypt again, now complete.
b: The bowls follow the order of the trumpets: land, sea, rivers, sun, darkness, Euphrates, storm. The trumpets struck a third; the bowls strike all. Sores were Egypt's sixth plague (Exodus 9:8–11), and they fall on those who carry the beast's mark.

a: you have given them blood to drink
p: They poured out blood; they receive blood.
b: The angel calls this just because the punishment matches the crime. The pattern of "measure for measure" runs through the book: Babylon receives the cup she mixed (18:6), and the destroyers of the earth are destroyed (11:18).

a: they refused to turn away from their sins
p: Three times the bowls note people refusing to repent. Repentance was possible.
b: 16:9, 11 and 21 note that people curse God instead of repenting, just as in 9:20–21. If the plagues were only punishment, there would be no reason to note that people refused to repent. My reading: even the last judgments in Revelation are designed as a final appeal, like the plagues of Egypt, which were meant so that "Egypt will know that I am the LORD" (Exodus 7:5).

p: For John’s readers, the Parthians. For later readers, many candidates.
b: Rome's eastern rivals the Parthians crossed the Euphrates more than once, and the Nero legend said Nero would return with them. In history and in the 20th century, readers have suggested Muslims, Japan, China, or other eastern powers. Cyrus took Babylon by diverting the Euphrates (Herodotus 1.191), and Isaiah 44:27–28 links the drying of rivers to Cyrus.

a: three evil spirits that looked like frogs
p: Egypt’s second plague, and a symbol of unclean things.
b: Frogs swarmed Egypt (Exodus 8:2–7), and Egypt's magicians copied the sign. Frogs were unclean animals (Leviticus 11:10). Some Persian texts call frogs creatures of the evil spirit Ahriman. Three spirits come from the three mouths of the dragon, the beast and the false prophet.

a: Look, I am coming like a thief!
p: Right before the kings gather, Jesus speaks directly to the reader.
b: Verse 15 breaks the scene with a beatitude about staying awake and keeping your clothes on, which echoes the warnings to Sardis (3:3–4) and Laodicea (3:18). My reading: John puts the call where you would least expect it, at the battle, because the real fight at Armageddon is about the reader staying faithful, not about military strategy.

p: Har Megiddo, "mountain of Megiddo." But Megiddo is a hill on a plain.
b: It is not a word that means "the end of the world." NASB prints it "Har-Magedon." Oddly, Megiddo is a mound on a plain, not a mountain. Suggestions include nearby Mount Carmel, where Elijah faced the prophets of Baal, or a play on Hebrew har mo'ed, "mount of assembly," where the king of Babylon tried to set up his throne (Isaiah 14:13).
orig: Ἁρμαγεδών (Harmagedōn), from Hebrew har Megiddo, "mountain of Megiddo"

p: The Greek says the weight of a talent, roughly 75 to 100 pounds.
b: A talent was a large weight, roughly 50–100 pounds depending on region. Josephus says that during the Roman siege of Jerusalem the catapults threw white stones weighing a talent, and that the watchmen shouted "The stone is coming!" (Jewish War 5.270). Preterists see this as the fulfillment; others read a supernatural storm, as in Exodus 9:24 and Joshua 10:11.

a: the great prostitute who sits on many waters
p: Jeremiah said this to ancient Babylon, which sat on the Euphrates.
b: Jeremiah 51:13: "You who live by many waters and are rich in treasures, your end has come." Babylon sat on the Euphrates and its canals. 17:15 explains the waters as nations. The prophets often called idolatrous cities prostitutes (Isaiah 23:16–17 of Tyre; Nahum 3:4 of Nineveh; Ezekiel 16 of Jerusalem).

p: Is "Mystery" part of her name? The Greek allows "a name, a mystery."
b: KJV prints "MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT" all in capitals, as if "Mystery" is part of the name. The Greek can mean "a name written, a mystery," meaning a symbolic name (compare "symbolically called" in 11:8). ESV: "a name of mystery." It warns you not to look for a city that is literally named Babylon.

a: drunk on the blood of God's people
p: Nero’s persecution in AD 64 killed many Christians in Rome.
b: Tacitus (Annals 15.44) describes Christians in Rome being torn by dogs, crucified, and burned as torches in Nero's gardens. Peter and Paul were remembered as martyrs there. Preterists who read Babylon as Jerusalem point instead to Matthew 23:35–37.

p: Every ancient reader knew which city sat on seven hills.
b: Rome was "the city of seven hills" (Latin poets: Virgil, Horace, Ovid, Martial). A coin of Vespasian shows the goddess Roma reclining on seven hills. The angel adds that the heads are also seven kings, so the image is doing double duty.

p: Which emperors? The count changes the date of the book.
b: Starting from Augustus: Augustus, Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius, Nero (five fallen), Galba or Vespasian (one is), and so on, depending on whether the three short reigns of AD 69 count. Starting from Julius Caesar shifts the list. Some say the seven are not emperors at all but seven empires (Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, Persia, Greece, Rome, and one to come), the common futurist view. Others read seven as a symbol of the full line of rulers.

t: An eighth who belongs to the seven
p: Eight is the number of resurrection in early Christian thought.
b: Early Christians called Sunday "the eighth day," the day of the resurrection (Barnabas 15:9). The beast "once was, now is not, and will come," a parody of God who "is, was, and is coming" (1:4). My speculation: the "eighth" king is a counterfeit resurrection, a revived old power posing as a new beginning. Interestingly, the Greek letters of "Jesus" (Iēsous) add up to 888, which some ancient Christians noticed (Sibylline Oracles 1.324–30), compared with the beast's 666.

a: Lord of lords and King of kings
p: Deuteronomy 10:17 and Daniel 4:37 in the Greek.
b: Deuteronomy 10:17: "the LORD your God is the God of gods and the Lord of lords." In the Greek version of Daniel 4:37, Nebuchadnezzar calls God "Lord of lords and King of kings." The title appears again on the rider in 19:16, in reverse order.

p: The beast turns on the city that rode it.
b: The beast and its allies destroy the prostitute. Evil in Revelation is self-destructive, and God "put it into their hearts" (17:17). Preterists see Rome destroying Jerusalem; others, Rome burning in AD 64 or AD 69 (when the Capitol was burned in civil war); futurists a future betrayal. My reading: the scene shows that the economic system (the prostitute) and the political power (the beast) are allies of convenience, and the second will devour the first.

p: Isaiah and Jeremiah pictured fallen Babylon as a haunt of wild creatures.
b: Isaiah 13:21–22; 34:11–14 and Jeremiah 50:39 describe Babylon and Edom becoming deserts haunted by owls, jackals and goat-demons. Ancient Babylon did become ruins, mostly abandoned by the 2nd century AD.

a: Come out of her, my people
p: Jeremiah 51:45: "Come out of her, my people! Run for your lives!"
b: Jeremiah 51:45 and Isaiah 48:20; 52:11 call the exiles out of Babylon. Paul uses similar words for separation from idolatry (2 Corinthians 6:17). The reason here is to avoid sharing her sins, which suggests a spiritual and economic leaving, not only a physical one.

p: The boast of ancient Babylon in Isaiah 47.
b: Isaiah 47:7–9: "You said, 'I will continue forever, the eternal queen!'... 'I will never be a widow.' Both of these will overtake you in a moment, on a single day." Revelation copies the boast and the "single day."

p: Chapter 18 is modeled on Ezekiel’s funeral song for Tyre.
b: Ezekiel 26–28 laments the trading city of Tyre: kings, merchants and sailors mourn, throw dust on their heads, and ask, "Who was ever like Tyre?" (27:32). Ezekiel 27:12–24 lists Tyre's cargo, like 18:12–13 here.

p: Slave traders called slaves "bodies." John adds: they are human lives.
b: In Greek commerce, sōmata ("bodies") was the standard word for slaves. John adds "and human souls," quoting Ezekiel 27:13, where Tyre trades in "human beings." The cargo list ends with the item that exposes the rest. Rome's economy ran on slavery, perhaps 10 to 20 percent of the population.

a: a boulder the size of a large millstone
t: A stone thrown into the river
p: Jeremiah had a scroll tied to a stone and thrown into the Euphrates.
b: Jeremiah 51:63–64: "When you finish reading this scroll, tie a stone to it and throw it into the Euphrates. Then say, 'So will Babylon sink to rise no more.'" Jesus spoke of a millstone tied around the neck of anyone who harms little ones (Matthew 18:6).

a: The voices of a bridegroom and bride will never be heard in you again
t: The bride moves to another city
p: The wedding voices leave Babylon and are heard again at the Lamb’s wedding.
b: Jeremiah used this line for Jerusalem's ruin (Jeremiah 7:34; 25:10). In the very next chapter, the wedding of the Lamb is announced (19:7). My observation: the book takes the bride and the wedding music away from Babylon, and moves them to the new city, which is itself "prepared like a bride" (21:2). It is a tale of two cities, and of two women.

p: Its only uses in the New Testament are here, four times.
b: Hallelu-yah means "Praise the LORD." It occurs four times in 19:1–6 and nowhere else in the New Testament. Psalms 113–118 (the Hallel) were sung at Passover, and Psalm 104:35 ends with the first hallelujah of the psalter, right after a prayer that sinners vanish from the earth.

p: The prophets called Israel God’s bride. Jesus called himself the bridegroom.
b: Isaiah 54:5: "Your Maker is your husband." Hosea 2:19–20: "I will betroth you to me forever." Jesus called himself the bridegroom (Mark 2:19–20) and told wedding banquet parables (Matthew 22:1–14; 25:1–13). Paul applies it to Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:25–32).

a: the right things God's people have done
p: "Righteousness of saints" is plural: righteous acts.
b: KJV: "the fine linen is the righteousness of saints." The Greek is plural: "the righteous acts of the saints" (NKJV, ESV, NIV). The verse also says the linen was "given" to the bride to wear (edothē). So it holds both together: a gift, and a life lived out.
orig: τὰ δικαιώματα τῶν ἁγίων (ta dikaiōmata tōn hagiōn)

t: Even John got it wrong, twice
p: The book’s visionary bows to an angel, twice. A warning about being dazzled.
b: John falls before the angel here and again in 22:8–9. The one who saw the vision was overwhelmed by its messenger. Several scholars suggest it warns against angel worship (compare Colossians 2:18). My application: if John himself could misplace his awe, readers should be humble about their interpretations, and keep worship on God alone, not on the prophecy or its interpreters.

p: Christ’s white horse answers the conqueror of 6:2.
b: Romans celebrated a triumph with the victorious general riding a white horse. The rider's eyes and sword repeat 1:14–16. He judges "with justice," from Isaiah 11:4.

p: The robe is bloodied before the battle starts.
b: Isaiah 63:1–3 pictures the LORD coming with garments stained from treading the winepress of his enemies. But here the robe is already dipped in blood before any fighting, and the armies following him are in clean white. Many scholars (Caird, Bauckham) read the blood as Christ's own. I agree: the Word of God conquers as the Lamb who was slain (5:6), and the only weapon used is the sword of his mouth (19:15, 21).

p: Ezekiel 39: a feast for birds over Gog’s armies.
b: Ezekiel 39:17–20: "Call out to every kind of bird... come together from all around to the sacrifice I am preparing for you." Revelation sets this "supper of God" against the "wedding supper of the Lamb" (19:9). Every reader is invited to one of the two meals.

t: Gehenna and the lake of fire
p: Jesus spoke of Gehenna, a valley outside Jerusalem.
b: The "lake of fire" is unique to Revelation. It draws on the fire of Sodom (Genesis 19:24), Isaiah 66:24, Daniel 7:11 (the beast "thrown into the blazing fire"), and Jesus's Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom where children had been sacrificed (Jeremiah 7:31). 1 Enoch 90:24–26 has fallen angels thrown into a fiery abyss.

p: A literal future reign, the church age, or a golden age before Christ returns?
b: Premillennial: Christ returns first and reigns 1,000 years on earth. Amillennial: the thousand years is the present church age, with Satan bound by Christ's victory (Matthew 12:29). Postmillennial: the gospel will spread and bring a long golden age before Christ returns. The early church had both premillennial (Irenaeus) and non-literal (Origen, later Augustine) readers.

p: Jesus said he had come to tie up the strong man.
b: Jesus: "how could anyone break into a strong man's house and seize his goods, without first tying the strong man up?" (Matthew 12:29). Amillennialists read 20:2 as that binding, with Satan unable to "lead the nations astray" (stop the gospel) during the church age. Premillennialists note that Satan is very active in the New Testament (1 Peter 5:8), so the binding must be future. Compare Isaiah 24:21–22, where powers are imprisoned "and punished after many days."

p: Beheading by axe was the Roman punishment for citizens.
b: The Greek pepelekismenōn refers to beheading with an axe, the old Roman form of execution. Tradition says Paul, a citizen, was beheaded. The word marks these as martyrs of Rome.

p: A bodily resurrection, or new life in Christ?
b: Premillennialists: a bodily resurrection of believers before the millennium, with the rest raised after. Amillennialists: either the new birth (John 5:24–29, where Jesus speaks of a spiritual resurrection now and a bodily one later), or the souls of martyrs entering heaven. The phrase "came to life" (ezēsan) is used of Jesus's resurrection in 2:8.

t: Gog of the land of Magog
p: Ezekiel 38–39: an invasion from the far north after Israel is restored.
b: In Ezekiel, Gog is the ruler of the land of Magog who invades restored Israel and is destroyed by fire from heaven (Ezekiel 38:22; 39:6). In later Jewish tradition, Gog and Magog became two peoples representing all the nations. Readers have identified them with Scythians, Goths, Huns, Mongols, Turks and Russia.

p: From Daniel 7:10: "The court was seated, and the books were opened."
b: Daniel 7:10 and 12:1–2 picture books at the final judgment. Judgment is "by what they had done," and yet entry depends on the book of life (20:15), the Lamb's book (21:27). Works show who people are; the Lamb's book shows whose they are.

a: Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire
p: The first thing to be destroyed at the end is death.
b: Death and Hades ride as the fourth horseman (6:8). Here they are thrown into the lake of fire. Paul: "The last enemy to be destroyed is death" (1 Corinthians 15:26). My reading: the lake of fire is presented as the destruction of the powers that ruin creation, which is why it is called "the second death." Whatever one concludes about its human victims, the text's first emphasis is that death itself dies.

a: a new heaven and a new earth
p: "See, I will create new heavens and a new earth" (Isaiah 65:17).
b: Isaiah 65:17; 66:22; 2 Peter 3:13. The Greek word for new, kainos, often means new in quality, renewed, rather than brand new. Debate: is this creation destroyed and replaced, or renewed (Romans 8:19–22)?

p: Sea meant chaos, the beast’s home, and the gulf between John and his churches.
b: The sea is where the beast rose (13:1), where Babylon's trade sailed (18:17), and where the dead lay (20:13). For John on Patmos, it also separated him from his churches. No more sea means nothing left that threatens or divides.

a: God's home is now with people
p: Skēnē, "tent," echoes the Hebrew Shekinah, God’s dwelling presence.
b: Skēnē means tent or tabernacle. It sounds like the Hebrew shekinah, God's dwelling glory, and its verb is used in John 1:14: "the Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us" (eskēnōsen). Leviticus 26:11–12 and Ezekiel 37:27 promise that God will dwell with his people. Note "his peoples," plural, in the best manuscripts.

a: He will wipe every tear from their eyes
p: Isaiah 25:8: "He will swallow up death forever."
b: Isaiah 25:8 and 65:19 ("the sound of weeping and of crying will be heard in it no more"). This promise was given to the multitude in 7:17, and now it is fulfilled for everyone in the city.

a: the names of the twelve tribes of Israel
t: Israel and the apostles in one city
p: The gates bear Israel’s tribes, the foundations the apostles.
b: The city is built on both: twelve tribes on the gates (from Ezekiel 48:30–35) and twelve apostles on the foundations. Many read this as the one people of God from both covenants. Some dispensationalists see Israel and the church as distinct groups who share the same city.

t: The size of the known world
p: 12,000 stadia is roughly the size of the Hellenistic world.
b: 12,000 stadia (about 1,400 miles) is a symbolic number (12 × 1,000). Several scholars note that a square that size would cover roughly the area from Rome to the Euphrates, or the Hellenistic world. My speculation: John's readers may have pictured the new Jerusalem as large enough to cover all their known world, so the holy of holies becomes as large as the empire it replaces.

t: Jewels of the high priest and of Zion
p: The high priest’s breastplate, and Isaiah’s jeweled city.
b: Exodus 28:17–21 has twelve stones engraved with the names of the tribes. Isaiah 54:11–12: "I will build you with stones of turquoise, your foundations with sapphires... your gates of sparkling jewels." Tobit 13:16–17 also imagines Jerusalem rebuilt with gems.

t: Pearl gates and the pearl of great price
p: Jesus told of a merchant who sold everything for one pearl.
b: Pearls were the most valuable gems in the Roman world. In Matthew 13:45–46 the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant who sold everything to buy one priceless pearl. My suggestion: John may want readers to recall that parable, especially after the merchants' lament over Babylon's pearls (18:12, 16). Babylon's merchants lose their pearls; the city of God is entered through them. (The "pearly gates" with Saint Peter as gatekeeper is later folklore.)

a: I did not see a temple in the city
p: The whole city is the Most Holy Place.
b: The city is a cube (21:16), like the Most Holy Place (1 Kings 6:20). Only the high priest entered it, once a year. Now everyone lives in God's presence, and "they will see his face" (22:4), which even Moses could not (Exodus 33:20).

a: the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it
t: The kings of the earth come back
p: The same kings who served Babylon now bring their glory to the city.
b: "The kings of the earth" committed sin with Babylon (17:2; 18:9) and fought the Lamb (19:19). Now they bring their glory into the new Jerusalem, as in Isaiah 60:3–11. Many scholars (Bauckham, Caird) see a note of hope for the nations here. My own reading is cautious: the text gives no timeline, but its final picture of "the nations" is of healing (22:2), not destruction.

a: the river of the water of life
p: Ezekiel 47: a river flows from the temple and heals everything.
b: Ezekiel 47:1–12: water flows from under the temple, growing deeper, making salt water fresh, with fruit trees on both banks whose leaves heal. Zechariah 14:8 and Psalm 46:4 ("A river! Its channels gladden the city of God") join in. Genesis 2:10 has a river flowing out of Eden.

p: In a city with no more pain, the leaves are still "for healing the nations."
b: If there is no more pain (21:4), why healing? Some read it as a picture of fullness of life, others as a continuing process. My speculation: the leaves answer the curse of Babel and of the nations' long war against God. The nations arrive in the city with histories that need healing, and the tree from Eden provides it.

a: There will no longer be any curse
p: Genesis 3 began with a curse. Revelation ends with none.
b: Genesis 3:17: "the ground is cursed on your account." Zechariah 14:11: "Never again will it be destroyed. Jerusalem will be secure." The Bible's story ends where it began, in a garden, with the curse removed.

p: Moses could not see God’s face and live. Here everyone does.
b: Exodus 33:20: "You cannot see my face, for no human being can see me and stay alive." Psalm 17:15: "I, in the right, will look upon your face." Jesus: "Blessed are those whose hearts are pure, because they will see God" (Matthew 5:8). The name on their foreheads recalls the high priest's gold plate (Exodus 28:36–38).

a: Do not seal up the words
p: Daniel was told to seal his book. John is told not to.
b: Daniel 12:4: "Close up and seal the words of the scroll until the time of the end." John is told the opposite, "because the time is near." Preterists stress that the nearness was for the first readers. Others see "the time of the end" as having begun with Christ (Hebrews 1:2; 1 John 2:18).

p: KJV "do his commandments" follows a different manuscript reading.
b: KJV: "Blessed are they that do his commandments." The oldest manuscripts: "Blessed are those who wash their robes." Written in capitals with no spaces, as scribes wrote, the two look alike: ΠΛΥΝΟΝΤΕΣΤΑΣΣΤΟΛΑΣ and ΠΟΙΟΥΝΤΕΣΤΑΣΕΝΤΟΛΑΣ. A tired copyist could slip. "Wash their robes" ties back to 7:14.
orig: πλύνοντες τὰς στολὰς αὐτῶν vs ποιοῦντες τὰς ἐντολὰς αὐτοῦ

p: A harsh word for people outside the covenant, used by Jews and by Paul.
b: Dogs in the ancient Near East were scavengers, not pets. The word was an insult for the unclean or for pagans, and Deuteronomy 23:18 may use it for male temple prostitutes. Paul uses it for false teachers (Philippians 3:2). The list matches 21:8.

p: Isaiah’s root of Jesse and Balaam’s star from Jacob, together.
b: "The Root of David" comes from Isaiah 11:1, 10 (see 5:5). "A star will march out of Jacob" is Balaam's prophecy (Numbers 24:17). The morning star was promised to Thyatira (2:28); now Jesus says he is that star.

a: The Spirit and the bride say, "Come!"
t: Who is being called to come?
p: "Come!" is said three times: to Jesus, to the hearer, to the thirsty.
